title: Archives, Cron Jobs, and the Shell Environment
intro: Backing up a directory, scheduling it to happen nightly, and understanding the environment it runs in — three small skills that combine into one very common real task.

steps.prompt: Create a compressed archive of /opt/myapp/data named data-backup.tar.gz.
steps.fake_output:
tar: Removing leading '/' from member names
/opt/myapp/data/
/opt/myapp/data/users.db
/opt/myapp/data/uploads/
steps.explanation: c = create, z = gzip, v = verbose, f = filename (must come last, right before the name).
steps.why: The 'f' must be immediately followed by the archive name — 'tar -cvfz' would try to create an archive literally named 'z'. Memorizing 'czvf' to create and 'xzvf' to extract avoids the whole class of mistakes.

steps.prompt: List what's inside the archive without extracting it, to verify the backup.
steps.why: A backup you've never verified isn't a backup. Listing contents is the minimum check; actually restoring to a scratch location and testing it is the real one.

steps.prompt: Find the full path of the tar binary — cron needs full paths.
steps.explanation: which shows the exact executable your shell would run.
steps.why: Cron runs jobs with a minimal PATH (often just /usr/bin:/bin), so commands that work fine interactively can fail silently under cron. Using absolute paths in cron jobs removes that whole class of bug.

steps.prompt: Check what your current PATH contains.
steps.explanation: Directories are searched left to right when you type a command name.
steps.why: This is the interactive PATH. Cron's is far shorter — comparing the two is exactly how you debug 'works when I run it, fails from cron' (see linux-incident-005).

steps.prompt: Open your crontab to add a nightly job.
steps.explanation: '0 2 * * *' = minute 0, hour 2, every day. The % in date must be escaped as \% inside crontab, or cron treats it as a newline.
steps.why: Redirecting output (>> log 2>&1) matters: without it, cron's output goes to local mail nobody reads, so failures are completely invisible.

steps.prompt: List your crontab to confirm the job was saved.
steps.explanation: The job is installed for your user.
steps.why: Never edit crontab by editing files under /var/spool directly — 'crontab -e' validates syntax on save; 'crontab -l' is the safe way to read it back.
